utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Do you hear me well, Mr. Galic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, good morning. I hear you well, and I also understand you in my own language. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, General. I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to start today by going back to some of the things you said yesterday and asking you a few more questions. Yesterday, I asked you whether you received information from the Main Staff about shelling and sniping by your forces into Bosnian-held Sarajevo, and you said that this could have been possible via Indjic. So I'd like to know about your communications now with Dr. Karadzic. Did Dr. Karadzic ever convey to you any information or reports or protests he'd received about the shelling and sniping of civilians by your forces in Bosnian-held Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, during the examination-in-chief, I spoke about that. I said that President Karadzic and I and the others, Akashi, et cetera, took part in this conversation when there was this agreement on the 5th -- or, rather, 18th of February, 1994. And then I received that agreement from him, and there was also an accompanying order as to what should be done in that area. When I recall the rest, now, there were questions like whether this or that was done, but not particularly in terms of carrying out combat tasks and activities, but I remember that he called me when I arrived at the command post. And when the problem of Markale I was supposed to be resolved, he called me then and I said we had such and such information and that we would check that then. So that would be it. Also, I said during the examination-in-chief -- well, possibly with regard to some humanitarian issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So apart from the situation you've just discussed related to Markale I, Dr. Karadzic never told you about any reports or protests or information he'd received from whatever source saying that SRK forces had been shelling and sniping into Sarajevo causing civilian casualties.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, such a conversation or such an order - yes, say order - from the president, I don't remember having received that. But at different discussions -- well, that was discussed, that there was a disproportionate use of artillery and that it should be decreased. Now, I don't know to what extent, but I also complained about that, and I cannot exactly define it. It seems to me that it was disproportionate, but I could not regulate that problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So what you're saying now is that there was a discussion in which Dr. Karadzic told you he'd received information that your forces were using artillery against Bosnian-held Sarajevo in a disproportionate fashion?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't -- well, how do I put this? It wasn't that kind of typical information. For instance, let me give you an example. I would like to portray this for you how this communication developed between the corps commander and the commander -- rather, the president -- or, rather, the Supreme Command. When he toured the corps, when he came to the corps command, he talked to officers and to me, too, and all these problems were referred to, and the problem that we're discussing now as well. He always said that attention should be paid, because before that there were some orders from the government forbidding any kind of firing at town and so on and so forth. I mean, this order arrived before I came as commander, but it was still in force. I cannot tell you to what degree. I've already said yesterday these cease-fires and orders, especially cease-fires, they would be in force until they were violated, and then also there were time limits.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thanks, General, but maybe we need to go back to what you said originally. You said -- your indulgence. You said at different discussions it was discussed that there was a disproportionate use of artillery and that it should be decreased. Was that Dr. Karadzic who told you that? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not to me directly. When he talked to all of us at the command, it wasn't that he called me and said, "I'm issuing such and such an order." No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I about transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Galic received interpretation of lines 3 and 4 that his forces were against the Bosnian forces in Sarajevo and the transcript says "Bosnian-held Sarajevo." So General Galic was satisfied with the question, so he did not refer to what was said there, Bosnian forces. The Serbian interpretation that he received was: "Your forces against the Bosnian forces in Sarajevo." And the transcript says that this is against Sarajevo. So since he did not get the right interpretation, he could not say anything in reference to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Edgerton asked her question again now, and then I think it's clear from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General, that instance where Dr. Karadzic told all of you at the command that there was a disproportionate use of artillery and that it should be decreased, when was that?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I spoke about a meeting that was held at the corps command sometime in 1993, but the date I do not recall. Around that time. I mean, when I said this, I spoke about that meeting that was attended by President Karadzic together with the corps command. So we discussed all the problems, all the other problems and - how do I put this? - the problem of disproportionate use. I do know that there was pressure from all sides in that domain, not only from President Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you say you know that there was pressure from all sides in that domain, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean all the mass media of the world, because I said to my soldiers and officers that if any shell falls, people know about it immediately in Washington and they say that we only targeted civilians, and that the newspapers are writing about that and so on and so forth. There is this Satanisation of the entire Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, thereby the Army of Republika Srpska. Let me also say that that is why we asked --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How about if we go back then to what President Karadzic said. You said that he told you and your staff this sometime in 1993. When in 1993?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember exactly. I said that I do not remember, but there was this meeting that I remember that was held at the corps command. It had to do with something. Now, whether it was the president going to the airport or something like that -- you're asking me now about something that happened so many years ago. I really do not recall the date. But that is true that he did have talks with the command, the corps command. Not these meetings that are part of protocol and that we discussed at higher levels. We've already had documents about that. But as for this meeting that I'm talking about, there's not a single document, at least not so far. It would be a good thing if you had a document and if we could see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, were you about to raise this translation issue about Satanisation? We'll correct it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in your two years of service in the corps command, was that the only time that Dr. Karadzic raised this issue with you?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've said -- I mean, I've already answered that question. There were other meetings, too, with me and with the other commanders at the level of government, at the level of the Supreme Command. Different issues were raised, including the question of what could be done in that domain to decrease this disproportionate use.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How often did Dr. Karadzic tell you that your forces were using artillery in a disproportionate fashion against Bosnian-held Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at every one of these top-level meetings, and I've already given this example of the corps command. It's not that he'd call me up every day and talk about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How often did every one of these top-level meetings happen?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I think it is already answered.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was it once every six months, was it once a year, or something more frequently? Can you estimate?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that topic was present all the time. Let's be clear on that. There was a war going on all the time, and there's always this evaluation, whether it's proportionate or disproportionate. There's fighting every day. Now, at which level what was discussed and how many times I discussed this with my officers, with my commands, how many times this was discussed at the level of the Main Staff or the level of the Supreme Command. It is certain that as the level is higher, the dynamics of raising such issues was greater, of course, because there are other problems in addition to that. There's not only Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So is -- can we understand you to be saying that Dr. Karadzic frequently raised this issue with you?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was raised because it was a burden on all of us, myself and President Karadzic. Let's be clear on that. There's no secret about that. And we were looking for a solution, how to resolve that, what to do. If you remember, when I said what the 1st Corps of the BH Army was given the opportunity to do and then also there were civilians there, 400.000 people. These are not small problem as far as the area of Sarajevo is concerned, if that's what you're talking about. So it wasn't only the problem of whether there was excessive use of artillery. There was a series of other problems that we discussed for five days, ten days, whatever. I can no longer recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And as a result of these discussions, what directives did Dr. Karadzic -- what did Dr. Karadzic tell you to do?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In relation to what?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In relation to the information he gave you that SRK forces were using their artillery against Bosnian-held Sarajevo in a disproportionate way. And Dr. Karadzic is quite right. I mean the city.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Could this please be stated very clearly to the General. Is it the city or is it military facilities, firing positions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. What -- I will read the question again for you. This is the question: "In relation to the information he gave you that SRK forces were using their artillery against Bosnian-held Sarajevo in a disproportionate way." And what was the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What did Dr. Karadzic to -- do in relation to this problem?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in relation to that problem, what we were asking for was quite clear. All of us, especially President Karadzic, Dr. Karadzic, to reduce this to a minimum related to military necessity and military objectives, that is a simple answer with regard to all these questions. I'm saying it wasn't every day that the president would call me up. I've already said there were other problems that had to be resolved, not only that one. Although this was a major problem for Sarajevo and it's a great problem for the 1st Corps of the BH Army and for me, too, for the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, that is. Well, it's hard to say here when you're talking about only one side and when -- I mean, when you're looking only at what one side did and you're not looking at the other side. For example, yesterday they did not allow people to go to Dobrovoljacka even now to pay homage to those people. Even now 20 years later they won't let people get in there, and we know all the things that Republika Srpska allowed. So giving a one-sided interpretation is a major problem, whether we ordered it, whether we did it sufficiently, whether we took measures and so on and so forth. We did order. We took measures that can be taken in wartime. Whether we should have done more, whether we had sufficient information about all of that, we've already discussed that. So I would kindly ask you to understand me along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Dr. Karadzic tell you that the disproportionate use by your forces of artillery into Bosnian-held Sarajevo had caused civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't have to tell me that. I -- I mean, everybody saw that, that there was a war going on and that fire came from both sides. During the examination-in-chief I spoke about that. I said that losses were possible and that they did happen. That's why I'm talking about disproportionate use, not any kind of intentional targeting of civilians, and that is the core of the problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you said, General, you took measures. What measures did you take? You took measures in response to the issue. What measures did you take?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already spoken about these measures yet again. I mean, I don't understand why you're asking about that again. I already spoke about it during the examination-in-chief. I gave an answer to the Presiding Judge as well. The Presiding Judge also put a similar question, measures that were taken by the units of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and by myself as commander. If you wish I have it written up here on five pages, all the things that we did. If you like, I can hand this over to you so that you can see all the things that were done, all the measures that were taken. I wanted to give that to the Presiding Judge at the end, because I owe him part of an answer to one of his questions. I said that we would deal with it later. It was stated later, but not everything has ever been said. These are two years of problems, two years of things that were being done, and after all, it is hard to put things in a systemic way in order to be as clear as possible. But basically, let me repeat what the basic things I did were. Madam Prosecutor, would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll ask the question a different way. Did you stop the disproportionate use, the disproportionate fire of your artillery into Bosnian-held Sarajevo? Did you stop it?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could stop that only in a situation if I were to stop the war but I, as corps commander, could not have done that. I consider such questions to be, well, unfair for a corps commander, whether I stopped that. I could not stop that. I told you how these casualties happened. This is collateral damage in a war -- or, rather, when there is firing in the Sarajevo area. And in this area where there is such a group of people, where there are provocations and so on and so forth. So -- I mean, for you to say, "Did you stop it?" I couldn't have. I could only have stopped it if I could stop the war as such. We suggested that the war be stopped in 1992 already. I think that that was when our Assembly passed a resolution on stopping the war. Maybe I'm making a mistake, but I know that once the National Assembly of Republika Srpska passed a resolution on ending the war. I thought that the war would be over then, and it wasn't over. In 1994, I left and the war went on for another year.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you told us yesterday that you removed two individuals from duty -- or you recommended two individuals be removed from duty, Dunjic and Grkovic, for, on the one hand, lack of discipline, excessive use of equipment, and so forth, but in fact, the removal of these two people had absolutely nothing to do with shelling and sniping of civilians in Bosnian-held Sarajevo, did it?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you always get involved in the same discussion, that only civilians were shelled and that Sarajevo-Romanija Corps fought against the civilians of Sarajevo and that is incorrect, Madam Prosecutor. If you just look at the losses that were there, if you look at what Ewa Tabeau said, and you will see what kind of losses the BH Army had. Where are these losses of the soldiers of the BH Army, 2.500 of them at that time point in time. We forgot to say that. We point out that there were civilian casualties. I agree, that should be highlighted first and foremost. But I've already mentioned that in Sarajevo, out of the total number of casualties in Sarajevo was 36 per cent. And then at the level of all of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a 600.000 concentration in a small area where there is a war going on each and every day, and at the level of Bosnia there are mountains where there's not a single person, but the average was 40 per cent, and they even said that 56 per cent was the figure related to civilian losses. I also presented some other figures. So I would kindly ask you not to put questions that way. Practically to say that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was not entitled to a defence, that the Serbs in Sarajevo were not entitled to a defence. I am not going to accept that no matter for how long I should be convicted. Well, convict me for as long as you want. Have me shot, executed, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, I was asking you only about Dunjic and Grkovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But when you referred to his earlier evidence, let's cite it correctly. Did he say shelling of civilians or sniping of civilians? So why don't we show the exact reference?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sure. Transcript pages 37811 to 37812.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What he's challenging is the shelling or sniping of civilians. So could you reformulate your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I will, and I'll get those pages up and read the General his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just before I reformulate, General, what you said in respect to Dunjic and Grkovic at 37810, actually, is that you proposed that the brigade commander be removed from -- a brigade commander and a battalion commander be removed from their positions. "The first commander, the brigade commander, lacked discipline, and he used equipment and assets that were excessive, and as for the second commander, I don't know whether I was right." And with respect to Grkovic, then at the next page, 37811, you went on and said: "He had to defend and protect Nedzarici. So any movement by such large forces that he expected would happen demanded that he engage as many people as possible to thwart those attacks, and that's why he always asked from the brigade commanders and his neighbours and he also sought approval from the corps command to perhaps engage artillery and heavy artillery assets, possibly in a more unproportionate way." All right. That's what you said. And, General, the reason why I'm asking this is Dunjic came here to testify, and gave evidence that his removal was actually as a result of a personal rift between the two of you, and he gave that evidence at transcript page 30486, and he even said that in November and December 1992, he had actually asked the Main Staff if he could be removed from duty on that same page. And in your own trial at transcript pages 47 and 48, Witness DP-4 said Grkovic was removed from his post in 1993 at the time when the Nedzarici battalion was amalgamated with the unit in Kasindol and the unit in the airport settlement to become one battalion, and another person was placed in command. And that's why I ask, their removal actually had nothing to do with shelling or sniping attacks on Bosnian civilians or civilians in Bosnian-held Sarajevo, did it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But General was correct that he didn't say that they were removed because of shelling or sniping of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Quite so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you're saying that attacks on Bosnian -- on civilians, but you reformulated. Attacks on civilians in Bosnian-held Sarajevo. Why don't you use his word, "disproportionate" or "excessive" use of artillery?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, did the removal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you for giving me the floor or thank you for having mentioned something because I was about to get on my feet. I would like to add that if General Galic remembers what happened in his trial, however, he knows not much about what happened in this case. I know how difficult it is to be clear, so if we are referring to testimony that took place in this case, it is important to read the testimony and not just say that on page 10800 -- 304. This is meaningless to the General and one has to provide the content of the previous testimony so that he can reply adequately. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think Ms. Edgerton faithfully and correctly cited the reference, and the reference page number is for the benefit of the Defence, not for the benefit of the witness, although it may be confusing to the witness. I think we can safely go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. And I'm sorry if I've confused you, General, but perhaps we can get back to this and you could tell us whether --

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not easily confused, Madam Prosecutor. People have tried to confuse me for 50 years already.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps you could tell us whether Dunjic or Grkovic were removed for use of SRK artillery against Bosnian-held Sarajevo in a disproportionate fashion.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last assertion is correct about the two of them, and that's the words that I used, disproportionate use of firing assets, including artillery. I am an artilleryman. That's -- I meant artillery. And I said about Dunjic that he did lack discipline. And it's only normal when a war goes on. He was engaged. He had his own views as to how to deal with certain problems. I did not consider whether he was right or wrong in his theoretical considerations, but I had a lot of objections to the practical side of his use of assets. That's why I thought that he would -- should be removed and not to have to deal with the problems that existed in his area of responsibility, and also because he used artillery and firing assets in a disproportionate way. When it comes to Grkovic, I don't know what Dunjic said here and I don't really care, to be honest. Let's be clear on that. I don't care what Dunjic said here. I know why a proposal was tabled for his removal. What he said is his problem. Everybody has the right to think for himself and to say whatever they want to say. That's the way he saw the problem, but I was a commander at the time. I had the right to make decision, and I proposed that he should be removed. I'm not hiding that. This is nothing new. When it comes to Grkovic and about his removal, I can tell you sincerely that it was not my doing. It was the organs of the command of the brigade and the authorities in the area that demanded his removal because he had been in a long -- in a bad situation for a long time. He -- he was stretched psychologically. I told you already that I went to Nedzarici on several occasions. Every time I went during the night and I would often lose my cap or some other parts of my equipment. So to live and to wage a war in Nedzarici was a sheer act of heroism. I believe that I mentioned it yesterday when I spoke about his removal that he did not have reserve positions. He didn't have anywhere to withdraw. He had to defend that Serbian area and the population in that area. It was a must for him. I don't know whether after that there was a reshuffling, a reorganisation, what activities ensued after that. This is neither here nor there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, now, both of those men were removed in early 1993. Were those the only two cases where you removed people from service for disproportionate use of your artillery against Bosnian-held Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, when decisions were made on personnel, you have to bear in mind a lot of things. I said that a lot was done based on my indicia about the disproportionate use of firing assets with regard to the military objectives that we wanted to achieve. Yes, there were other activities in terms of order and discipline which should have resulted in a more rational use of other firing assets. In the area of --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Before you go on to that, can you just answer my question? Those were the only two people you ever removed from service for disproportionate use of your artillery against Bosnian-held Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were the two commanders which were removed from their positions because of the disproportionate use of firing assets, and the reasons why I consider them to be disproportionate, I believe that I have belaboured the matter quite sufficiently. If you don't agree, I will go over the same ground again.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you consider something -- actually, I'll go to something else that you said yesterday. Yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you're moving away from this topic. General, we've been talking about the disproportionate use of artillery for some time, and you stated that Mr. Karadzic at one point in time about the -- about it, i.e., disproportionate use of artillery, and that it should be decreased. How did you understand the word "disproportionate," "disproportionate use of artillery" to mean? Could you give us some examples?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, an obvious example, Mr. President. It's very difficult to give you examples, but I shall do it. For example, what I observed and what prompted me to conclude and arrive at some indicia. If the enemy side, i.e., the 1st Corps of the BiH Army fired one shell, was it necessary to fire three, five, or six shells from our side? This is the disproportionateness in terms of achieving a military objective. If a commander was of the opinion that he had to destroy that firing position, there was no arguing with that because it was up to the commander who was in charge of certain assets or units. I couldn't tell him, "You should not have destroyed that. You should have neutralised it." It was a very difficult thing because I never crossed over to the other side to see what had happened there in order to make the right decision. We are talking about the disproportionate fashion. If they fired two or three shells on our positions and we responded with ten in turn, for me it is some sort of indicia that that was disproportionate, but I cannot prove as the corps commander that the brigade commander made an illegitimate or illegal - I don't know what word to use - inappropriate decision in any case. Whether that attack was legitimate or not, I can't be the judge of that, i.e., whether the fire opened was proportionate to the objective that somebody wanted to achieve. So that will be that. I believe that that was biggest problem, how to suppress all that. On the examination in chief I said that I had taken measures to control the spending of the artillery ammunition and that the artillery fire use should be approved at a higher level, which means that if fire was opened by a battalion, it would be the brigade commander who would decide on its use, but it was not always possible. For example, when an enemy had to be stopped and if that wasn't done immediately, the enemy could break through and the whole area would -- fell. To what extent could we ask for such an order to be carried out? These were all war dilemmas but as for the answer to your question, I would like to say that this was a problem, whether one should respond with a certain number of shells in response to a certain number of shells that were -- that had been fired at us. In very simple terms, that was up to every commander to decide.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I just -- about transcript. In line 11, 12, General said, "We did not have any depth," and it didn't -- hadn't been recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You mean on the previous page, page 17?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: No, no, no. It is this 18. Talking about "the enemy could break through." Prior to that he said, "We didn't have any depth."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you confirm having said that, Mr. Galic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a well-known thing. I've already said that several times. If you look at the map, the depth of our positions was perhaps 2 or 3 kilometres. That was all. The rest was under the control of the 1st Corps of the BiH Army, and I've said that on several occasions, but that was not in the entire area but in some parts of the zone of defence of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Back to you, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, we've been having this discussion with respect to artillery and artillery ammunition, but the same applies to the use of mortars and mortar ammunition by your forces, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you think that all of that is shelling, both things. So when we talk about this part, then we can also include mortar fire under that same category. In this indictment and in Annex 2 of my indictment - I don't know about this indictment - certain incriminated incidents and activities are mentioned, i.e., shelling, but those were mostly mortar shelling incidents. All the five incidents. Whatever I said about artillery also applies to mortars when it comes to the disproportionate use of those assets.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, as we look through some of the documents you dealt with in your examination-in-chief, I noticed one of them used the words "active defence," and that's one of your reports, and it struck me that we've seen that word in other documents from your forces. Are you in a position to explain what "active defence" means?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, I'll do that gladly. I'll tell you what this is about. Active defence implies that a certain area is defended, and some of the units are deployed in an area, whereas the other elements or the other units are trying to repair the positions in that area as it were. Active defence also implies situations where an enemy's trying to break through on an axing [as interpreted] and suppresses forces on that axis. The rest of the forces or neighbours will attack those enemy forces and help return lost positions. Active defence also depends on the focal points of activities. For example, some parts of the forces are engaged in defence, most of the forces are engaged in the defence, and rest of the forces are engaged in attack. In that case we're talking about active defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And we see in D3452, that's the document that provoked my question, we see this document refer -- uses the words -- the word "persistent defence" as well. Does that mean the same thing?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Persistent? Is it persistent or continuous? There is no "continuous defence" or "permanent defence" as a term used by the military. There is no permanent or continuous defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General -- General --

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was probably used in a different era or in a different century.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To avoid any lack of clarity, perhaps we could have a look at the document so you could see what word was used in your language.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's D3452, paragraph 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In English it reads -- it uses the phrase "persistent defence," and then in this paragraph I also see a phrase "preventive performance of offensive actions." What do they mean, General?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is an entire military theory but I'll try and explain in a nutshell. Persistent defence means that positions that are being defended must not be abandoned. They are defended persistently. An order may even be issued to defend those positions at the cost of a loss of life, a lot of life, and that persistence depends on the objective that was given to the unit in the area. It may be an operative objective or a strategic objective. It says here "preventive offensive against the enemy." What is "preventive" or "pre-emptive." If you think that the enemy will engage you in offensive activities, and we received information from those who crossed over, electronic surveillance, reconnoitering and other forms of security work. For example, we realised that the enemy will engage in attack. This is the most sensitive part of military activity. And before they launch the attack, they need to be attacked because they are focused on a different objective that they want to achieve, and you have an advantage because you can achieve more than in any other situation because you have an element of surprise on your side. This is pre-emptive action. The enemy doesn't -- actually, that preventive action does not cover a great depth, but its objective is to prevent the enemy activity in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just on this subject of disproportionality that we were talking about, I want to go to a transcript of an intercepted conversation between you and General Milovanovic. And it's P4782, on 20 May 1993, and it is an intercepted conversation that was reported by the Croatian Defence Ministry. Actually, it's a summary. It's a summary of an intercepted conversation. Now, in this conversation, you inform General Milovanovic about clashes your forces appear to be having with the Bosnian Army of -- at Grbavica, and you seem to say a large number of shells fell around the bridge area on 19 May. Now, General Milovanovic advised you to reply to each attack with a force five times greater, which he said will be justified as active defence. So does --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether the General is reading the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, I don't know if he can actually see it. It's rather faint.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. I really was not able to see anything, but now it is all right. So thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The concept of active defence as you've explained it, General, is something that General Milovanovic is telling you allows for a disproportionate response. So disproportionality is actually ordered by your military superior in this record of a conversation.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, this is the first time I see such a document, and I'm thinking about it now. What can I say when you see something for the first time 20 years later and you learn and wonder whether its true or not, to what extent is it true. And another thing, I asked to be given all the intercepts in my trial, but the Prosecution told me that it had no intercepts at all, not a single one that would contain something accusatory against me. It was not introduced during my trial. So this is something new for me. There were some other intercepts but not involving me. Whether Milovanovic told me this and why, I cannot answer that now, but I cannot even remember that he told me something like this. That's why the selection from which this part of the conversation comes, that I was issued such orders, I don't know. I don't remember. I don't remember. I cannot comment on this, because I don't think that -- this wasn't really Milovanovic's style, even though I could say many things now after everything that has happened, but I would not like to blame anyone, his role or his honour. I cannot remember that something like this was told. If I said it was in the sector of the bridge, it means that it was the Bratstvo i Jedinstvo bridge somewhere in the sector of Miljacka. That was where many shells fell, and he said that we should step up our activities, intensify them. I don't know why he said that. Perhaps he had some information based on which he told me this. What if he expected some sort of counter-attack of the enemy forces and therefore meant that we should intensify our activities. There are many conditions on the basis of which this could be interpreted. It would be the best if you invited General Milovanovic, he's your expert witness as he informed my Defence, and then you can ask him questions about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I know that the Chamber is paying much attention to fairness, but in this document there is no mention about the disproportionate nature. The question is based on the fact that General would have asked a disproportionate response, but we don't know the situation, and the General clearly said that it depends on the situation. We -- he can try to achieve an objective, but when it is considered from the answer that this is disproportionate, this is not fair. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure this is the subject you should intervene at the moment. Let me consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Rest assured the Chamber will conduct the trial as fairly as possible, and if there's some unfairness in the formulation of question, no doubt the Defence will raise it. So on that basis we can continue, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Let's continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you, General --

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not understood. I apologise, Mr. President. I have not understood the -- the interpretation. What sort of "natruha" or what it was? I have not understood the interpretation. So can you please interpret this once again. Mr. President, what -- what Mr. President, the Presiding Judge said. You were interpreting it and I haven't understood interpretation. The word something like "natruha" or something. Did I hear this properly? So I'm addressing the interpreters. This is a matter of interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I can't follow. Probably Mr. Karadzic can help the witness, or the interpreters. But what I said is, in a nutshell, that it is notwithstanding Mr. Piletta-Zanin's concern, we can continue with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there was one word that was used. It's possible that it's a Croatian term. I haven't heard it before in the Serbo-Croatian language. The interpreter used it, and when the interpreter was interpreting what you said in your response to Mr. Piletta-Zanin. That was why I asked it to be re-interpreted so that I could understand what you said, because I really haven't understood it. I'm following closely with much care what you said and especially your words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Active defence, as you've explained it, is something I want to stay with for a little while. Active defence was -- was core to the military directives your forces received from the Main Staff, wasn't it? It was fundamental.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for clarity, could you repeat your question? I'm not sure if it was translated correctly. Active defence was --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Active defence was fundamental to the directives your corps received from the VRS Main Staff, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is not so. Excuse me, but you asked me whether this is so, so I answered that it's not. But let me continue just so that we understand each other and that we don't improvise. The main thing for Sarajevo, only Sarajevo -- I'm talking about Sarajevo because the corps, as I said, had other fronts as well, which it had to have, but for Sarajevo it was always said "persistent defence." Persistent defence, not -- and in other parts it was active, active operations. There were periods when we would say "active defence" in some other areas but not so frequently. The expression "persistent defence" was used more often, prevent the enemy to break through and so on. If we agree about this. If not, I know what expressions were used and the directives which we received were termed like that in relation to Sarajevo. Use persistent defence to prevent and so on and so forth, rather than active defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So as -- so operations undertaken in persistent defence would not normally be the subject of daily reports because these were effectively operations undertaken under standing orders; correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, the operation is conducted by the entire corps or it can conduct it, and the other things are combat and battles which are conducted by smaller units, so as to make the distinction between operation, battle, combat, and so on. When we talk about operations, then the entire corps is supposed to be involved in it or the majority of the corps forces. In -- as for whether the defence operation, we can call it a defence operation in Sarajevo, in the Sarajevo zone, well, the focus of the forces was to be engaged in such a way that what you stated could be taken as true and correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to leave that and go back to one small thing that you talked about yesterday, and it's another explanation I want to ask you for, and it relates to the subject of -- it may relate to the subject of disproportionate. But yesterday you also indicated that sometimes fire was excessive and that's at transcript pages 37208 and 37209 [sic]. So you were talking about fire on Sarajevo, Bosnian-held Sarajevo, I take it.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The term "fire" implies -- we have -- when we talk about the problems of fire, there is a firing system. Infantry fire, artillery fire, too, the system of infantry fire, the system of artillery fire, the system of blocking. We have to take into account these systems. When we say "firing activities," that implies firing from all sorts of weapons. This is why we should make a distinction between what we are discussing. Or if we say "fire" or "firing activity," it means fire from all sorts of weapons. In what degree, what equipment, what weapons, that depends on what is used --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- at a single location along a single axis at a single point in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you said yesterday that sometimes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. The transcript page you refer to is part of yesterday's transcript? Probably the page number is correct or I -- it must have referred to the earlier dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry, 37208 is the earlier date, and 37809 - and I'm sorry if I've misspoken the numbers - is yesterday's transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So when you talked about fire sometimes being excessive, were you referring to infantry fire or artillery fire or mortar fire? What were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, Madam Prosecutor. In the transcript I'm not sure in the context of what I said that. I am following, but if we talk about firing activity, I explained prior to this that that implies fire from all sort of weapons. If I talked about infantry fire, then that only relates to fire from infantry weapons. If we talked about mortar fire, then I probably meant that. But if I said only firing activity, then it's universal. It applies to all weapons. Whether I have answered you -- I think that that's what it is, if it fits into the context of my answer from yesterday, or if you have more questions, let us be clearer if possible, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You were asked at 37809 whether there was any incident in which you answered admitting the SRK's responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was from me, Mr. Galic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It was from His Honour Judge Kwon. And you said, "I couldn't admit anything because I didn't have enough information so as to be able to admit to such an incident," and then you repeated that you didn't have enough information. And then later on in your answer to His Honour

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON YOU SAID
utterances.text: "Let me tell you, there were situations when I myself says that those reports that were received on excessive use of fire and firing equipment, that those reports were rather correct, and sometimes fire was excessive." So when you said "sometimes fire was excessive" in that answer, you were referring to mortar and artillery fire, I take it?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I meant any fire, but excessive means -- in that context it should be viewed as disproportionate, and that is my term, and that is the exact term based on what it is when we talk about forms of attack and so on. So there is a term. What is implied by disproportionate fire. Probably when I was explaining that, I implied under that term a disproportionate use of firing assets. Ones or the others, I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, let's just stay with that word that you used, that you actually did use a little bit. If fire -- if fire -- sometimes fire was excessive, was it excessive because of its effect on the target area?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we can try to guess now what, when, and where, but without a specific example I cannot give you a proper answer. I wouldn't like to speculate. I explained what I implied under excessive fire, and what is otherwise implied in the military lingo when we say "excessive fire." Excessive is something that is unnecessary, to put it simply. Too much fire is surplus fire, to try to rephrase it. And now how this is interpreted in accordance with the Geneva Conventions, it would be disproportionate.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was it excessive because it exposed civilians in Bosnian-held Sarajevo undue risk?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To what risk was the population exposed? Was it unnecessary or necessary? Was it collateral damage? Was it deliberate targeting or was it not deliberate? We could have discussed each specific incident and then draw such conclusions. To speak generally about this, it's imprecise in the first place, and it's not good. You keep insisting, and that was the indictment as well, that was the political view and the view in these trials in general, that we waged war against the civilians in Sarajevo. Whatever we did, we were carrying out a campaign of sniping and shelling against civilians, and we had no right to do that. This is why you are leading your questioning and phrasing your questions. That is why I find it difficult to answer such questions, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, I was asking the questions because you used the word, and you used the word on more than one occasion, but --

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, madam. I do not deny that I used it. I did use it. No doubt about that. But in what period, in what context, when, to what question? We can discuss that, whether the term was used properly or improperly, why it was used, under what conditions, in what situation. I'm not trying to evade saying that. Let's us be clear about everything. I have come here to say the truth so that people would learn something more about the war in Sarajevo. I've told you that. At least what I know. What I don't know and if I'm not certain about something, I will tell you immediately. I don't know, I'm uncertain, or I have forgotten and so on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Since you, General, find it so difficult to answer the question, rather than waste time I'll move on to deal with one final area before we break. I want to go back to a map that you looked at in your evidence in chief. That's D --

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree that it's difficult for me. I wouldn't say it's not difficult. I did answer your question, but the question is whether you have understood me, whether you want to understand me or you don't want to understand me, nothing else. I did give you an answer to the question, not only now but during the last five, six, or eight days during my testimony. This is not something new.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: As I said, I want to go back to D3383 from your evidence in chief, but what we've actually done is we've made a cutout of that map, which is 65 ter 24954, so that we can see it a little better. And I want you to help us with some of the symbols on that map. So that's the cutout, General, and we're going to be coming back to that. I just wanted you to see it quickly to refresh your memory. Now, I wanted to understand what these blue symbols denoted so I found a document, which is 65 ter 24949, and it's an excerpt from a JNA manual explaining various military symbols used on maps. And I looked at this manual to see if we could identify some of the symbols on this map.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So if we could see 24949, please. If we could go over to page 32, and it's not available in a translated form yet. And if we could turn it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The second item on page 32, that denotes a machine-gun, doesn't it? "Mitraljez." The second symbol on page 32 is for a machine-gun, isn't it, General?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's what it says here, that it's a machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the one --

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And these are --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The one immediately below that is an anti-air -- the symbol for an anti-aircraft machine-gun, isn't it? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When it has these symbols down there, yes, it's anti-aircraft machine-gun, yes, and it says 30/2. It means that the calibre is 30.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- the very bottom symbol is a symbol for an 82- or 60-millimetre mortar; correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. 120, it has one more there, up there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can we go over to page 38, please, of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, there's some diamond shapes on this page. Those denote different kinds of tanks, don't they?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There are these signs for a light tank, middle-sized tank, heavy tank --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- water tank and a tank for clearing --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's go over to page 42. That -- the symbols on page 42 denote different kinds of artillery, and the second item is a top field gun, the third item is an anti-tank gun, and the fourth item is a howitzer; correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if we go over finally to page 45, we see the second item is a symbol, as you mentioned earlier, for a 120-millimetre mortar; correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now if we could go back to the map that we just saw, 65 ter number 24954.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we are waiting, I will ask you, if you will ask me questions from the map, if we can zoom into one section so that I can see it because I don't see anything. When we see the whole map I don't see a single symbol. I just see that there's a little bit of red and a little bit of blue, but I don't see anything else. So if you could phrase the question in such a way that we zoom in to one section of the map. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No problem. Let's see if you can deal with my question. So using those symbols as a guide, General, I applied them to the map, and by my rough count, which is -- and I stipulate rough and conservative, I see that deployed around Sarajevo on this map you had approximately 40 tanks, 35 anti-aircraft machine-guns, 20 anti-aircraft artillery guns, 30 field artillery guns and howitzers, at least 50 mortars, some multiple-barrelled rocket launchers, I counted the symbols for 10, and 20 APCs. So -- now, General, that's your weapons surrounding Sarajevo. So you said in your testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The General wanted to see the zoomed-in map. Why don't we do that for him.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't have a particular question about a particular section, but we could do one section at a time so he could see the zoomed-in map. Or do half of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can scroll --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Ah, perfect. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, General, in your testimony, when you looked at this map in your testimony in chief, you said it was pretty accurate as regards the deployment of your forces facing theirs. So these figures I gave you, as I said accepting that they're only rough, but the figures and the weapons deployment as shown on this map of your forces would also be accurate; correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And so the General can see what I'm talking about, maybe we can zoom in or scroll around on the blue areas or the blue symbols on the map, so the areas outlining Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I don't see how the General can really answer that question because it's compound and includes two aspects: Does the map accurately represent the position of their forces; and second, is her calculations correct? I don't think that second portion can be answered by the General without studying the map. She's gone ahead and added things up and it seems to me that that's unfair to the General to ask him to accept that part of her question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did he not tell us that the map accurately represents the position of SRK positions during the direct examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. So I think that's about as far as he can take it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So if --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, no, no. I have an objection to that. I never spoke about positions of artillery pieces on this map, please. I talked about the deployment of forces and resources, but I did not speak about the deployment of the artillery pieces of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Of course I can provide answers to these questions. It's no problem for me not to do so, but if we recall correctly, this was a map that was drawn by the BH Army. I don't know who it was that drew this map, and these are their estimates and assumptions, and it's really the deployment of their forces. I discussed with President Karadzic then the deployment of their forces and I just mentioned in passing which forces of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps were there, without going into which artillery pieces were in which positions and when and so on and so forth. The Prosecutor is putting a general question to me, and I believe that that is allowed, in terms of what the situation was in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, how many tanks, APCs, howitzers, mortars we had and so forth. So these are different figures and different estimates and in different situations we had a different number. So that is why this is relative information, the information that you have. If you say that you counted the pieces here on this map, and that was my understanding, judging by what was marked on this map, I mean, I cannot say how many were marked on this map. I didn't count it, but if necessary, I can count it, but I don't think that would be necessary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you say this map was drawn by the Bosnian Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, maybe. It may have been drawn by the Army of Republika Srpska, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, but this kind of map --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Why don't we upload Exhibit D3383.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think it might be too big to be uploaded on e-court, Your Honour, which is why I made the cutout, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's do it first.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In my case it didn't take too much time. Do you remember this map, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember this map, and I remember interpreting what this was, the staff and the defence of Sarajevo, the defence of Sarajevo, something like that, and we interpreted it in a way -- I mean, it was my understanding that this was a map from the BH Army, from a BH Army source, not of the VRS. I'm sorry if I misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't think that someone in my corps had this kind of schematic. It would not have been logical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Back to you, Ms. Edgerton. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Two points. If there's the slightest doubt, in light of the map we saw last week, I have the original map. I've brought it back with me. If you feel it might be necessary, I can provide you with that, and I can rush back to my hotel and provide you with this original map if you need it. The General said that he remembered something and we have the opposite in the transcript, so there is an element of contradiction here. Please check tout.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for your kind suggestion. Let's see whether it's necessary or not. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So leaving aside the figures, taking on board what Mr. Robinson says, and leaving aside the figures, General, you said that this map, in terms of the deployment of your forces, was pretty accurate. Is this map also accurate then in terms of the deployment of your forces' weapons?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And maybe we need the zoomed-in one again so he could see that a little bit better, please. That was 24954.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. I believe that there is a bit of confusion here. Our forces are not marked anywhere here. It is only the forces that are in the defence that are numbered. It's written in the Latin script. It says that it's the units of 1st Corps. Our units, our forces are not marked at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you give the reference where the General testified that the map was accurate in terms of the deployment of the SRK.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Transcript page 31789.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you remember the date?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Leaving that aside, could you answer the question? If you remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first day. It was on the first day, this discussion about the deployment, and we discussed it on the first day. I don't know exactly what I said on the first day with regard to this, but I said something similar to what the Prosecutor said just now, but it had to do with the deployment of the Muslim forces and the other forces of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and that is basically correct, and I can repeat that now too.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it's 37189 as I inverted the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this is what you said: "This part of the map which depicts the deployment of our forces facing theirs is pretty accurate, pretty accurate." Although you "can't make it out that well, though, on this map." Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And my only question before we break is with respect to the weapons. With respect to your forces' weapons, then, General, is the deployment depicted on this map also pretty accurate?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pretty much, to put it as briefly as possible. Pretty accurate, but whether it's exactly that number and exactly in that location, that could be discussed. But pretty accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what I wanted to say: The General said that he could not read the maps that have been shown to me. He's been asked to provide a blanket statement in view of a series of symbols which he can't really see, and had I been in his shoes, I would have answered exactly the same way. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, would you propose that Mr. Piletta-Zanin would kindly bring the original map to provide the witness with this map or you can do without it?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In the spirit of fairness, we can have an enlarged cutout of what appears on the screen in front of us now made over the break for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Before we break, could I have 65 ter 24949, the JNA manual with the military symbols admitted as a Prosecution exhibit, please, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President. And probably limited to those pages which were used.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And we'll have it translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI P6301, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will have a break for half an hour and resume at 10 past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, you looked at a lot of documents -- oh, I'm sorry, General.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I've just received the map now. Sorry, I got a bit carried away.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You looked at a lot of documents, General, during your testimony in chief which Dr. Karadzic showed you as examples of restraint on your part in the face of violations or attacks, and I want to go to just two of those. The first one is D3386, and it's dated 26 October 1992. And we can have a look at it. And in respect of that document, at transcript pages -- you discussed that document at transcript pages 32716 to 32719 [sic], and in that discussion, Dr. Karadzic asked you why you didn't open fire on Sarajevo, although the document is silent as to action your forces might have taken, and you said: "On the whole and in essence our forces for the most part, irrespective of the existence of an order to cease-fire, as we'll see later, mostly refrained from firing because whenever we responded and whenever we did anything, there was a general outcry." So even though the document is silent, your evidence is that you didn't open fire on Sarajevo that day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid that this is misleading. It's not correct that it's not written there. It is stated where this firing took place, and there is no firing at the city, point 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you give the transcript page reference again?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The discussion was -- I've given the range for the discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I think you said 32716. I don't think it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, I'm so sorry, Your Honour. That would be 37216 to 37219.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, General, to get back to my question, your evidence is your forces didn't open fire on Sarajevo that day. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the 26th of October, 1992, so let us go back to the year and the time when this situation was there, the one that is presented in this report to the Main Staff. On that day we noted here where fire was opened and in which areas. That is stated in paragraph 2. The forces in the area of Osmice on the slopes of Mount Igman, attack from the Famos factory was repelled. So that's the Famos factory, and so on and so forth. So what we wrote here was where we had fired. These forces that had fired and what was noticed was practically that they fired at Ilidza, and we see what the losses were down there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, General --

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major losses. Yes, yes. I'll get to the answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My question was --

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- did you open fire on Sarajevo that day?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never opened fire on Sarajevo, Madam Prosecutor. I opened fire not on Sarajevo but on enemy forces. Let us be clear on that and do not put questions like that to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we please have a look at 65 ter number 24965. It's an excerpt from the Commission of Experts report which says at the bottom of page 18 what happened that day. There should be -- if we could go to the bottom of -- e-court page 18. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, it's in English, unfortunately, General, so I'll read to you the last paragraph on the bottom of this page with a report on what happened on 26 October 1992. It says: "Sarajevo was relatively quiet overnight. However, Serbian forces in the hills unleashed a loud artillery barrage on the Dobrinja apartment complex" - if we could go over to the next page - "near the airport in the morning. Heavy shelling rocked Sarajevo's western suburb of Stup around midday and mortar rounds fell on a district near the UN headquarters in the city, wounding 5. The western suburb of Dobrinja was also a target for heavy fire during the morning. At least 5 people were wounded by a single mortar round, 4 of them seriously." And then further it says: "UNPROFOR reported that a total of 43 heavy artillery rounds hit Bosnian-controlled areas around Sarajevo and 7 hit Serb-controlled areas in the 24-hour period ending at 5.00 p.m. on Monday. "In the 24-hour period that ended at 10.00 am Monday, 4 people were killed in Sarajevo and 47 others were wounded." So your evidence just now was that you opened fire not on Sarajevo but on enemy forces. Are you saying that this report of events represents your fire on enemy forces?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report is a report of United Nations -- excuse me. Now, to claim on the basis of that, whether fire had been opened at Sarajevo, to speak about Sarajevo that way, in this wholesale manner, that's a popular thing to do, but these are completely different concepts, opening fire at a city and opening fire at enemy forces, and that's why I'm a bit upset by that. I cannot interpret here whether fire had been opened at the forces of the 1st Corps of the Army of BH, but if we look at the areas that they refer to and the deployment of forces of the 1st Corps of the BH Army, we cannot say or assert that fire had not been opened at the forces of the 1st Corps of the BH Army. On the other hand, this claim in our reports and my statement in relation to what the report to the Main Staff was, I mean, I stated the information that I had, or, rather, whoever wrote that report. So which are the reports that are correct? Which are the ones that are doctored? How was this information received? I wouldn't want to go into all of that. We did look at all of that during my trial, and we saw that these reports were inaccurate, too, in part, not all of them, because they were received in different ways.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on, then, General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I don't think this is a report of United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Pardon me. It is not. It's an excerpt from the Commission of Experts report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The Commission of Experts was a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we have evidence -- did we hear evidence about that commission and its activity?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Nothing immediately comes to recollection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So to put the content of the witness, I think it's fair to introduce what this document is about and it footnotes some press clippings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, actually that -- I think -- I was going to make that same point. What this actually is just a compilation of press clippings of newspaper articles. Whether it was experts or whoever I don't think is that relevant but what actually this is is some kind of compilation of newspaper articles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm overlapping. I couldn't see the cover page of this document so that's why I asked that question. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And again, taking on board what Your Honours and Mr. Robinson -- taking on board what Your Honours and Mr. Robinson have said, I'll just move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could look at another document, General, D3410. It's a report that Dr. Karadzic showed you, dated 4 February 1993. And I'll just provide the transcript page cite in one second. And you discuss that document with -- you discussed that document with Dr. Karadzic during the first day of your evidence. Dr. Karadzic -- Dr. Karadzic said to you, in regard to this document, that it reflects the situation at 1800 hours that day. It says that the attack commenced at 1700 hours with 120-millimetre shells targeting Nedzarici from the direction of Dobrinja and the Olympic village. That such a combined artillery and infantry attack was still going on, and that your focus was on reconnaissance and observation of enemy activity. And he asked you: "What does this mean that you're not returning fire yet but you are only observing and reconnoitering?" And you said: "If I go back to that time of 4 February 1993, I'm sure there must have been specific reasons why we did not respond to this sort of fire and risk to our territory which was exposed. I suppose that there was a specific reason why we did not want to return fire at once. I suppose that in the meantime a protest was lodged with UNPROFOR that the BiH Army should desist." And that was at transcript pages 37335 to 37336. So, General, my question is: Is your evidence that you -- your forces did not shell Bosnian-held Sarajevo that day?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, I can claim that on the basis of what I read here, because to remember something else in relation to that day compared to what I see from the reports and to the Main Staff, that would be unfair on my part, because I can certainly not interpret it any other way than what is written here. After all, it was signed by my deputy, Colonel Marcetic, and that means that that is the situation. They say that they did not respond to enemy fire, although we see down here -- actually, there was this question put by President Karadzic. Wasn't that reason enough? A child had been wounded. You know what my answer was in that regard. It is sad. Every loss is sad, but particularly the loss of children, but we have to know what the price would be if we were to respond in terms of fire against the BH forces, especially bearing in mind what the objective is with regard to this firing.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So your evidence is that you have no recollection as to whether or not your forces shelled Bosnian-held Sarajevo that day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Please, could Madam Edgerton be asked to state precisely what she means by Bosniak parts of Sarajevo? The witness already said that these questions were not correct or fair. He should say which parts of Sarajevo and what the objectives are. In my view these are trick questions, if you will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I don't agree with you in that regard, but I would ask Ms. Edgerton to reformulate her question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you have, then, General, any recollection as to whether or not your forces fired on encircled Bosnian-held Sarajevo that day, on the 4th of February, 1993?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have already spoken with regard to that term "fired on." I don't want to go over that again. I know -- I know what you're asking me and I want to repeat my previous answer. I cannot say anything different than what is written in here. Twenty years later I cannot remember the day, and I'm not in a position to say anything differently than I see in the report. I really would like to see a genius of that kind who would be able to do that. I'm sorry for answering in such simple terms.
