However, if that is what is in the report, if that was drafted and signed by my deputy, Colonel Marcetic, I can only say that I agree with this report, nothing else, because I don't have any other information. I didn't it then, I don't have it now. Obviously you must have a document or a report speaking to the contrary of what I can see in this report. Okay. Let's discuss that. Let's discuss your document, because I cannot say, as I sit here, that I remember things in a way different to what is stated and described in the report that is on the screen before me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, was that the case with all the daily combat reports you were shown in your evidence-in-chief, that you actually have no independent recollection of the events they describe and were drawing your answer from what you saw on the pages in front of you?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you provoking me here? I believe you are. I've already answered you. If you understood my answer, if you are willing to understand my answer, perhaps your understanding of people is different. Maybe you are exaggerating the abilities of a human brain. I'm saying that there are events which I remember. There were such events. But asking me to remember exactly what happened on a certain day, whether it was foggy, whether it was raining, there had to be an event to jog my memory to that effect. I can tell you that I went to the Nisic plateau and that it was snowing but I don't remember the date. And it's not even remember. Yes, I do remember things but I can't remember everything, madam, and I'm sorry that I have to respond in this way because any other answer would be improper on my part. I told you that I was a sincere and honest man. I want to arrive at the truth together with you, and if you think that I'm lying here, just tell me so. You can tell me, "You are a liar," but this is not my intention. I'm telling you what I know. What I don't know, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Then, General, perhaps I can ask you a question about something that, since you mentioned it in your testimony to me yesterday, you might have some knowledge of. Yesterday you said that Bascarsija was a museum area and shouldn't be targeted, and that's at transcript pages 37836 to 37837. So, General, you're familiar with the Old Town of Sarajevo, I take it.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, we discussed Cengic Vila and the incident at Cengic Vila, that's when I answered your question in that way. Cengic Vila is called Cengic and that name is based on history, and I drew a parallel and I compared Cengic Vila to Bascarsija. I will tell you what happened to me --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, General, can you just answer my question. You're familiar with the Old Town of Sarajevo, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I want to answer you. I don't know what you want from me. I want to answer you, and you are not letting me answer you. This is my style of talking. We should finally be on the same page after all. It is true that I said that Bascarsija was spared our attacks and now I'm sure that you want me [as interpreted] to show a document that will prove that Bascarsija was fired on. I can only guess how to answer your questions so that I do not refute my own words and you would then tell me that I am lying, and I'm not lying. I can only misunderstand your questions. Please bear that in mind. I told you that Bascarsija was spared [Realtime transcript read in error "compared"] because in a certain way it is a symbol of Sarajevo for both Serbs and Muslims as well as for Croats. Let's be clear on that. And for myself it was a symbol. It was something that represented Sarajevo in everybody's eyes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you're denying that the Old Town of Sarajevo was ever shelled by your forces?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, just a second. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I must intervene here because I'm only relying on my memory, but if my memory serves well, General Galic said earlier on that he was not from Sarajevo, that he didn't know the city in details. He said that very precisely, and I have the impression that he's guided into another way now, saying something that was different from what he said yesterday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Than what he said earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- for the Serb translation I didn't say "yesterday" but I said "earlier on."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What I wanted to say to you is that, with due respect, I find this intervention not very helpful. If the General is not familiar with the geography of the central area of Sarajevo, he will testify so. So could you kindly refrain from making substantive comment about his testimony. The Chamber will look to it with utmost care. By the way -- yes, I'll leave it. Let's continue. Do you remember the question, General, or shall I ask Ms. Edgerton to repeat it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I remember the question. There's no need for the question to be repeated. I remember as much. But it's not about my -- the question but the way I'm answering and what kind of answer Madam Edgerton wants me to give. That's the problem. I'm answering in my own way. She's looking at things from the legal point of view and I'm looking at things from the military point of view, but we will arrive at the truth after all. Let me answer. I didn't say the old part of the city. That part of the city up there, Sedrenik from the centre upwards, that's what it's called, and it is not that only Bascarsija was the old part of the city or the municipality in that city. The municipality was more than just Bascarsija. I spoke about Bascarsija as a symbol, as a part of Sarajevo which is still a symbol of Sarajevo. It always was and it always will be, and it was spared. There was no activity in Bascarsija. I wanted to tell you when I toured the front line and when I checked whether the soldiers knew that they were not supposed to open fire on that area at all costs, they said, "Yes, of course, Bascarsija is protected and should not be fired on." And that's the answer I got from my soldiers. You did not allow me to say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, my question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Before you --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the record, transcript page 48, line 67, "compared" should read "spared." "I told you that Bascarsija was spared because in a certain way it is a symbol of Sarajevo," not compared. That's what I heard, and I note nodding by the witness. Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, my question was actually about the Old Town. So my question is: Are you denying that the Old Town of Sarajevo was ever shelled by your forces?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not denying that. I just told you that Stari Grad is an entire municipality. It is a part of Sarajevo. Take a map of Sarajevo and you will see the inscription "Old Town" and that includes Bistrik, Bascarsija, and the entire north-eastern part of Sarajevo or even the northern part of Sarajevo. That is Stari Grad or the old city. That's the municipality. You're asking me whether that was spared, i.e., whether it was ever shelled. This is a very wide question and it refers to a wide area. I am answering you that I don't know when and which part of that municipality came under artillery fire and what enemy forces were fired on in that part of the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You said it's a very -- it's a wide area. Now, tell us what's the radius of that area of the Old Town? Because you seem to be quite familiar with it from what you've just described.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, I think that comment should be avoided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you tell us the radius, then, of the Old Town, General?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's take a map of Sarajevo and let's see. Let's look at a map, let's see where it says "Stari Grad," and let's calculate.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is your evidence, then, that you don't know the radius of the Old Town and the areas you've described, General?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, I'm not sure if you -- the witness and you are having the same thing in mind when you refer to Old Town. So could you clarify with the witness first.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, the area that includes Bistrik, Bascarsija, and Stari Grad that you've just described, I'd like you to tell us how big it is, the radius, please.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, Bistrik is part of Stari Grad. Stari Grad is a municipality. I'm talking about municipalities. There is the Centar municipality, the Novo Sarajevo municipality and the Stari Grad municipality. Look at the map and you will see what they encompass. So when you see the inscription "Stari Grad," it's not just that territory. The municipal territory -- or, rather, the city of Sarajevo had ten municipalities, and the municipality of Stari Grad is somewhat broader and covers more area than you see on the map. That's why I ask you if you have a map of Sarajevo, let's look at it, and let's define the boundaries of the Stari Grad municipality. When you mention Stari Grad I'm not talking just about one facility or feature. I'm talking about the entire territory of the municipality. Do you understand what a municipality is? If you do not, let me explain. And I've told you already what municipalities there existed in the whole area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, rather than spend more time on this, you talked about Bistrik, and you talked about Bistrik in your evidence in chief. You explained to Dr. Karadzic that you shelled Bistrik, and that was at transcript page 37359. And you also noted that Bistrik was a populated civilian area. How many times did you shell Bistrik?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You drew a lot of assertions about Bistrik and you're asking me just one thing, and now it is impossible to answer that question, how many times fire was opened on that area where force -- the forces were deployed. And you know that it was the 10th Brigade that was deployed there. Later on it was the 105th Brigade. Originally it was the 10th Brigade, and it constantly attacked the area leading up to Trebevic. How many times fire was opened on the enemy forces, I don't know. Fire was opened, yes, it was. I base my answer on the report that you have in front of you that fire was opened on Bistrik. I agree that there were a lot of civilians there, a lot of civilian facilities. I don't know what else you want me to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. So now you've just talked about civilians and civilian facilities in Bistrik. I just want to look at a couple other areas of town. Alipasino Polje, that's also a civilian area, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, if you put it that way, the entire city of Sarajevo is a civilian area if you look at if that way. Before the war, Sarajevo was a civilian area, all of it. Alipasino Polje which is close Goranovo Naselje, Dobrinja, and so on and so forth, and there is a part leading towards the Miljacka, Alipasino Polje is there. At that time whether Alipasino Polje was a civilian area, look at this map here and you will see what units were deployed in Alipasino Polje, and now you are claiming that this was a civilian area. Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, Nikola Mijatovic from the Ilidza Brigade came to testify in Dr. Karadzic's defence, and at transcript page 30737, he said Alipasino Polje was a civilian area. I'll ask you about another area. Ciglane, that's a residential area, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please let's go back to Alipasino Polje for a brief moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you know -- do you know -- do you know where the Kulin Ban Unit was deployed? If this is the way you want to discuss things, let's discuss them in that way. Do you know where the Kulin Ban Unit was deployed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, General, it's not a discussion and I'm afraid it's not for you to ask the questions. If necessary, Ms. Edgerton can rephrase her question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My question was about Ciglane and whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You made a comment about Mr. Mijatovic's statement, I think it's fair for the witness to make any comment about that. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I? I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You disagreed with what alleged Mijatovic's statement or testimony. I will leave it to Ms. Edgerton whether she wants to ask more questions. Otherwise, Mr. Karadzic will take up that issue, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, do you agree that Ciglane is a residential area?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't say. I don't know if Ciglane was residential or not. I remember a moment in time when the Prosecution suggested that there was an incident in Ciglane involving artillery fire and we established that tanks were deployed there, and as soon as that happened, the Prosecution immediately gave up on that incident. I don't know whether my answer was good, whether I made myself clear, I don't know. And when it comes to that unit, Kulin Ban, it was deployed in Alipasino Polje and that is the area where the incident happened -- happened involving children. And Mr. Piletta-Zanin always liked to ask questions about Kulin Ban and the deployment of that unit and now I can answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, Dusan Skrba came to testify here in Dr. Karadzic's defence, and at page 29144, he said that Ciglane was a residential area exclusively. Would you have any reason to disagree with him?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, let me repeat why I don't agree with that. Those are his observations. Mr. Skrba was an artillery commander. He was assigned to a brigade. I was the corps commander and I knew things, and when I say something, I base my words on what I know. I explained to you how I saw Ciglane at the time. Whether there was a period of time when there were no troops deployed there, I don't know. If you can prove that, fine. I tried to prove to you why you gave up on that incident in my trial, in my proceedings. If I'm lying, please tell me so; if I'm telling the truth, again, why don't you tell me that I'm telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, would you agree that Velesici is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I'm not sure the General said -- and I'm talking about page 54, line 19, and I hope that this will help the Chamber. I don't think that he said that there were no troops deployed there. I think I heard he said the opposite. He said that there were tanks deployed there, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's continue. Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would you agree that Velesici is a residential area with family homes and apartments?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every part of Sarajevo was residential. There were civilians and soldiers in every part of Sarajevo. Some were in Velesici. But let me remind you of a daily report and you will see that fire was opened from Velesici towards Stari Grad. That was my daily report, if I remember it well. And if fire was opened from Velesici, that means that there were troops there at that time. They were deployed in depth towards the centre of Sarajevo and towards the railway station. That's Velesici. On the side is Trbaceva Kosa [phoen] and up there is Hum. Whether there were troops in that area or whether all of the people there were civil -- civilians is a matter of discussion. We can go on discussing that. I would not agree that everybody was civilian over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can we look at a document now? It's P1009, and it's a document dated 11 October 1992 from Radislav Cvetkovic, your chief of artillery, to the command of the 4th Mixed Artillery Regiment and Anti-tank Regiment. Now, this document says that -- you see, in respect of points 1 and 2, it's issued further to an order by you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And we can scroll down the document so the General has a chance to see it, and then eventually go over to page 2, paragraph 3 in both languages, where it refers to the firing tasks of the artillery.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are we okay to go to the next page, General?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course. This document is out of my range. This was a document that the chief of artillery was authorised to sign and make an independent decision on the contents thereof. If you are seeking my comment on the document, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll come back to what you've just said, but you see at the top of this page where you see paragraph 3(c), it lists among the artillery tasks to prevent the enemy's attack aimed at lifting the blockade of Sarajevo by opening fire at the areas of Hum, Pofalici, Velesici, and lists a couple of others, Jarcedol, Colina Kapa, Stup, Alipasino Polje, and Mojmilo. And then at the next paragraph it says: Support the counter-attack by our forces sending fire into the regions of Trebevic, Colina Kapa, Bistrik, Radava, Pionirska Dolina, and so on. And then from its basic firing position, it says that the corps artillery group supports -- supports by sending fire into the regions of Ciglane, Kobilja Glava and Bistrik, Kozija Cuprija. So first of all, General, can you confirm that this is a firing plan linked to a corps-level operation because it refers to an order you issued planning attacks on regions and areas that -- some of which your subordinates have confirmed are residential.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, you have to make a distinction between several moments here. In my order I gave a general task to the artillery. This means I'm planning things that they have to carry out in the zones of their defence. The chief of artillery here puts forth planning part or the possible attacks by the enemy and where fire should be opened. This doesn't mean that fire was indeed opened but that fire has to be planned on certain sectors, on certain axes, and in certain situations. Where it says, "prevent concentration," "prevent attacks," these are his assumptions with regard to the axis along which we expect the enemy to try to break through and that's how we planned the fire. This is the way things are done in artillery. These are tasks that are given to artillery. It's only normal. To go on saying that this area is a civilian area -- and let me tell you, the plan was drafted for the time when BiH Army were deployed there. If no BiH units were deployed there, there would be no fire. So let's draw a very clear line between a plan and the actual execution thereof. I can go on but let's not waste time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it would help if we were to read all the paragraphs from this (c). I think that would explain many things and that we would shorten the time, especially this under "neutralise," "neutralise."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document was admitted in connection with the evidence of Mr. Philipps and I would ask now that it be admitted for all purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was trying to locate all the passages we read out. It's part of firing tasks? Are they all part of firing tasks?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Under paragraph 3. I only have the B/C/S in front of me at this moment. Three --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Top of page 3 in English says: "Neutralise the enemy's artillery by opening fire on the area of Velesici," et cetera. Does this mean that there's something military set up in Velesici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that period it could mean so but not necessarily. That is the axis along which a movement of the BH Army -- of the 1st Corps of the BH Army was expected, along that axis, so the tasks had to be with regard to the axis, because via Velesici, you go on to Zuc and Brijesce Brdo where activities would be carried out. And that was where he expected some forces to come by. If they were to come by to Velesici, he planned some fire; for example, to concentrate fire in order to prevent the enemy from passing through that zone. Mr. President, was that sufficient? But please, you wanted to see the axes. Can you please remember what I said about the areas where we expected active combat and the breakthrough of the 1st Corps of BH Army troops at the positions of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. If you compare, you will see that these are the axes where we expected increased pressure or breakthrough from the forces of the 1st Corps of the BH Army. This is the best way to understand this plan of the chief of artillery or, rather, the order on the use of artillery. I think that that's the title but I don't remember precisely. Mr. President, that would be all unless you have any more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Exhibit P1009 will be admitted in full.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have a look at P2656, please, which is dated 26 November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it's another firing plan, General, if you could look at the screen, from Radislav Cvetkovic again. And it says, as did the first document, that items 1 and 2 are the same as in the order by the SRK commander. And then in paragraph 3, subsection (c) --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So we'll have to go down the page in B/C/S, and 3(C) is at the bottom of page 1 and then over to page 2 in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Paragraph 3, subsection (c), is, General, identical to paragraph 3(c) in the first document. So, General, it looks to me like what we have here are effectively standing orders in terms of firing plans. The plan of fire hasn't changed from one month to the next.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The plan can be changed from one second to the next, but the adaptability of the plan is its greatest value. It has to be adapted to the given situation or -- which arises. I have told you that the main characteristic of each plan is such and so is the plan for artillery or its use, because I issued one order and on the basis of that order all other organs are drafting their own orders, depending on what their task is. Or they make plans, calculations, and all the other staff duties are carried out on the basis of my basic order. Likewise with this order issued by the chief of artillery. It can be changed somewhat. I cannot compare the two texts now to see whether they're identical. There would be no reason to send out two identical texts, but if something is to be stressed out, the particular commander can refer to his own order such and such a number, as it was usual for me, and then something new is added as well. So this is an order pursuant to which further plans on the use of artillery would be made. This is an order setting out the plans only. It's not realistic that all of this would be achieved, but there has to be readiness to achieve it if needed, which in turn depends on the activities of the enemy. In a war, you try to foresee the enemy activities and that's the greatest value of each commander, the ability to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General, can we have a look at 65 ter number 24952, and you talked about an order that you issued within which particular commanders would develop their own orders, and this is an order dated 26 November 1992. So it's the same date as this second artillery plan that we saw. And if we go over to the very last page, you can see that it's signed by you; correct? Is this -- is this the operational order, the order for further activities, operation 11/92, that formed the basis for the artillery plan we just saw, the firing plan we just saw? And if we go over to the first page again, you can have a look at it to familiarise yourself with the document.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not necessary for me to look at the document for a long time. I'm familiar with it. It is my order. I think it's the first order that I issued in the corps. Unless I'm mistaken, but I think it's the first one. Because when I arrived, there were many things in the corps that were not well, not even the orders. They didn't know that there should be directives by zones, and I wanted to define many things in one of my order, many obligations of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, does this order -- does this order relate to the firing plan we just saw?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But does it include artillery tasks? There should be an item with that title "artillery task" -- "artillery tasks." If it's not there -- I'm not sure. It could be a bit more extensive not just this one page. I think it could have as many as 17 pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can we scroll slowly through this document for the General, because artillery tasks aren't under one specific heading. They're broken up through the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me explain, Madam Prosecutor. That is stated through the tasks of brigades so as to see whether the corps artillery would support them or not. That is why the artillery tasks are repeated several times, but for each brigade, whether they support them on the particular axis, the brigade has to know whether the corps artillery supports it or not and in which situation. This is the reason why these tasks of this artillery are repeated several times or the 400th MAP. That's what I meant. Was I sufficiently clear about this? But artillery tasks are there. There must be a separate item that states the artillery tasks. I don't know if you asked me now. You can see the date here, but it has to be included. I don't see it now. It's not in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you go to the next page in the document, please. And the artillery tasks heading that the General is looking for is paragraph 6.2, but unfortunately, I can't tell you what page it is in B/C/S at this moment. It's page 13 in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 9 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Could it be printed and given to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's see whether it's necessary. I doubt it. Page 9 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Great. Thank you. Heading 6.2, "Artillery Tasks" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we show the top part as well. It's very short. Scroll up, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So all I wanted to know is, General, is does this operation order from you relate to the artillery plan we just saw? Or is the artillery plan a standing order?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order was written, and its value is long-term. It is valid up until the next order or a supplementary order. It can be supplementary or a new order with a new operational number, just like with directives. The procedure is the same. The general tasks of artillery support are set out here. I do not specify those details. That was the duty of the chief of artillery and other chiefs who were members of the staff, namely, to specify specific tasks for their specific units. I just set out what were to be the focal points of activities of the artillery, and further development and -- of the plans was up to the chiefs or their deputies depending on the levels. It can be the deputy for intelligence and security, but this one was the chief of artillery because he's a member of the staff and so on. So these are long-term tasks. Up until a moment when the order is issued with the changed tasks. On the basis of this, the chief drew up his own order and probably some plans for the artillery activities, whether he was the one who made it or not, and that would include also a map and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is your answer then, "Yes"?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you phrased the question in such a way that I cannot say just yes. Yes to what? I'd like to be able to understand what exactly you are asking me? So please -- excuse me for asking you once again to ask me. Yes to what?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Does that artillery plan that we just saw relate to the order, the operations order, that's on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a plan what we saw. It's an order on the use of artillery and the plan is something different. So this order was issued by the chief of artillery, and it is in accordance or it should be in accordance with what I wrote here with regard to artillery and its tasks. If it's not in accordance with this, then it means that the chief of artillery missed the point.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could that be a Prosecution exhibit, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6302, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You've repeated in your testimony, General, that your forces only shelled sources of enemy fire within the front lines, inside the front lines, when you were fired at, and that's at a number of transcript pages: 37204, 205, 37239 to 40, and 37335, and 37219. I would like now, General, to show you a video, and it's a very short one, and I'm going to ask you some very specific questions after the video.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the video for the record is at P1933, and our colleagues in the interpretation booth should have a copy of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: "...When they arrived they were told that Vedrana had already been buried half an hour early because the graveyard was being shelled by the Serbs."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could pause. I'm not hearing any interpretation yet. Could our interpreter colleagues confirm that they've received copies of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, we have received it. Should we read out the text which is read out in the video?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, it's in English and I take it -- and I take it it was being translated into French and B/C/S. That's why you didn't hear that. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, that's not the issue. If you allow me, I have 30 minutes -- seconds. I would like to say that this question is a misleading question. The General stated a while ago that in certain cases, he could intervene in a pre-emptive way. So when one says that he only responded to the source of fire, this is not correct. He said sometimes a surprise effect was good and it was good to act in a pre-emptive manner. One needs to be very concise when one asks these questions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpreters in the booth on the other side of the courtroom haven't been provided with a copy of the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. General, did you hear the interpretation of this video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I heard something. I don't think it was fully what was said. I don't know. I'm not sure what's necessary. This is the first time I'm watching it, but I heard that they arrived immediately after the Serb shelling. That was what I heard in interpretation, and I don't know the rest. This video could be from a location -- from any location, anywhere. This is just something that was filmed. It's not telling me anything. Judging by this, Vedrana, judging by the first and last name, could also be a Serb woman. She doesn't necessarily have to be a Muslim woman. She could be a Croatian. I don't know. I'm watching it but I would like to reach the appropriate answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The video's original soundtrack has been hardly audible so far. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We'll try to again, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: "When they arrived, they were told that Vedrana had already been buried half an hour early because the graveyard was being shelled by Serbs. That was bad enough, but it got much worse. More shells started falling. One landed as the boys and girls from Vedrana's children's home arrived with their flowers. As quickly as they could, they dropped them on the graves of Vedrana and the baby boy the sniper also murdered. It was time to go. As the family was leaving, the gunners found their range."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does this seem to you as an original video that was shot during the war?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tell me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This video was made by BBC journalist Jeremy Bowen at a funeral in Sarajevo. Now, I have two questions for you from the clip that you've seen. Did you see any outgoing fire from this funeral?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I'm sorry that something like this was -- happened, but it looks to me something that was fabricated later on. It looks like something that was rigged. It's not possible. It just doesn't happen this way. What was made here, whether it's some smokescreen or something -- there was firing everywhere, perhaps even here too. I do not deny that. That was something that was mentioned in my trial, firing from Mrakovo and so on. Then we saw that there was a mortar, an enemy mortar at the graveyard itself, and now to say here whether some outgoing fire can be seen here. You see the person who came there to film it, these were people who came deliberately to spread propaganda, the cameraman, and I think that the whole scene is rigged, in my view. The children coming with flowers, then fleeing. I don't know if this is really how it all happened. It's possible that it did. But it does not seem very realistic, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My question, General, was: Did you see any outgoing fire while you were watching this video?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it is really the time to take into account what the witness says. He refused to accept that this is authentic, and he expressed his opinion that this was all rigged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That it was staged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But he also said it's possible that it happened, but I don't see the point of your question. If outgoing fire had existed at all, it could have happened before this clip.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, I acknowledge that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. So shall we move on, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine. I just note it's 12.26, Your Honour. I wonder if you would like to take the break now, and then I would probably be a part of the next session but definitely not the whole session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I have a matter that I'd like to deal with in the absence of the witness, so, Mr. Galic, if you could be excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I won't find that very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, while the witness is leaving the courtroom, I would like to thank the Prosecution for having specified this issue. I'm trying to change my flight for tonight, and if everything could be finished today, that would be wonderful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's a message to Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's a clear message to Mr. Karadzic. Would you like me to leave the courtroom also? [In English] Do I have to stay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oui, s'il vous plait. I'm going to discuss something confidential to our case, so if you could excuse yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was for the witness. No problem. I shall leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Could the Chamber move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And before the next witness testifies, I'd like to hear from the parties as to the relevance of paragraphs 42 to 47 of that statement. And there's one minor housekeeping matter. The Chamber recalls that on the 27th of February, 2013, it instructed the accused to redact part of paragraph 12 as well as paragraphs 27 to 32 of Exhibit D3031, which was the statement, witness statement of Milovan Lelek. The Chamber now wishes to clarify that instruction and order that the accused redact paragraph 26 to 32, not 27 to 32, as well as part of paragraph 12 of that exhibit. The Chamber also takes this opportunity to remind the accused to complete any pending exhibit issues as soon as possible, including the redaction of numerous pending witness statements. We will have a break for -- yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Just one other housekeeping matter. Yesterday we filed a motion for an order to the Deputy Registrar pertaining to medical records for Milan Babic and we'll withdraw that in light of the Chamber's oral ruling yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take a break for 45 minutes and resume at quarter past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To move on, General, to another area, could we have a look at 65 ter number 24959, please. General, this is a document you sent to all SRK units on the 9th of February, 1994, regarding the movement of artillery. And it says that overnight -- it directs the troops to overnight between the 9th and 10th of February move defective weapons towards Sarajevo -- can you see it, General, or does it need to be enlarged?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite frankly, I cannot see it, so if it could be enlarged. Thank you. Thank you. This is already better. Because after all, this text it quite illegible.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So it's to move defective weapons towards Sarajevo and take up fire positions, and if the cease-fire is signed, these defective pieces, it says, are to be moved out in daylight so UNPROFOR could see it, and that way basic weapon systems remain on vital positions. And paragraph 4 of this document says: "In the event of NATO air-strikes, attack, imprison, and hold UN and all humanitarian organisations until the air-strike ceases." Now, this is your document, General, and at transcript page 37448, you said that you complied with the total exclusion zone agreement to the last letter. If you ever did anything fully and completely, it was this. Your own document from the time, General, shows that you had no intention of full compliance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to underline that, as far as I remember, General Galic was never worried nor condemned for adopting behaviours towards NATO staff or UNPROFOR staff, and this issue might involve Mr. Galic's responsibility pursuant to Article 90, if I'm not mistaken. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for the reminder, but I remember that I gave him the advice pursuant to Rule 90(E), i.e., his right to refuse to give his evidence if the testimony is to be --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: But before that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I'm trying to remember the word of the Rules, but I'm just carried away.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Mr. President. You are not carried away at all. I know it off by heart. Article 90(E).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The word I was trying to remember was "incriminate." I'm very sorry. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think in our system this would not have been allowed, that the witness be led through the question. This is the 9th of February, and the agreement was signed on the 18th. You cannot say on the basis of this that General Galic did not observe the agreement. On the 9th there was no agreement yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, it goes either way. I don't see any difficulty with the General being capable of answering this kind of question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I specifically referred to an intention to -- the General not having an intention to comply. I'm quite aware that the agreement wasn't signed at that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Galic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask you to be able to have a look at the signature at the bottom of this document. As far as I can see, there is no signature here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it this is a telegram, Mr. Galic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as far as I can remember, I was not at the corps command then, and that's why I want to see who signed this and why this kind of order was issued. I'm not deciding yet at the command post who issued this order to them and how, that is something I cannot interpret now, but this is what I would like to say: At that time, as has already been stated and is well known, I mean, we said during the examination-in-chief that the agreement was reached only on the 18th, so your statement, Madam Prosecutor, that I did not intend to implement the agreement -- well, from this we cannot see that there is no intention. I say here that all resources should be prepared. Preparations are already underway. But there is this warning down here. I don't know whether it's good or not. Well, maybe it's a bit excessive, that if there were to be NATO air-strikes, then everything would go down the drain, and then -- well, it has to do with the attitude towards UNPROFOR, not to kill them. That is stated there. That is sufficient protection vis-a-vis them. Although, this process, how it would evolve, to tell you the truth, I don't find that clear. But if there is bombing, then chaos reigns. The question is how all of this would be carried out altogether? Well, perhaps we can say that this is a preparatory order for what would follow on the 18th or, rather, the 19th. I think that later on our dead-line was the 19th by 2400 hours. So everything that had not been withdrawn or notified, then there would be bombing. That's my answer. I don't know whether it suffices.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The General said if there is bombing, then everything goes down the drain, all the agreements. All the agreements would no longer be in force, and that was not recorded, that the agreements would no longer be in force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm having said that, Mr. Galic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I confirm that that was said, Mr. President, because practically that's how it would have been. I don't know. While I was commander I wasn't told -- I mean, well, how it was later, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have this document, please, as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6303, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General, I'd like to show you another document of yours dated 20 February 1994, and that's D2802. And it's a regular report from you to the VRS Main Staff on the situation that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And perhaps we could go all the way over to the last page so that the General can see who signed the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's your signature, isn't it, General?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No doubt. My signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if you go in this document to English page 2, and the reference in your language is on page 1. The last subparagraph --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think it's on page 1 of -- no. If we could go to the next page, please, in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this page is fine. You can see the meeting with Akashi.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I've again written my numbers incorrectly. It's the last subparagraph of section 23.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: There is no 23. Could you please read it, and I will instruct -- I'll say what is the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Karadzic, for your help. And I apologise for my inability with anything to do with numbers. "In order to prevent a surprise, parts of units with their private weapons were kept in full combat readiness with enhanced measures of surveillance and position maintenance."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The penultimate and ultimate of page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you. We have that page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just before -- the paragraph before number 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General, in commenting on the previous document, you said that that didn't show any lack of intention on your part to comply with the agreement. And now this document is dated the 20th of February, 1994, so after the agreement is signed, and you're telling the VRS Main Staff that you actually haven't complied. To prevent a surprise, parts of units have kept their weapons in full combat readiness.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, you did not understand this right. I'm going to explain this to you, and then we are going to get a different conclusion from the one that you've drawn just now. Actually, at all these locations where weapons were collected at that point in time, that they had to be transported, you have to know that there's lot of snow then, that movements are highly restricted. It was total disarray, not to go back to all the bad things that happened then. However, these weapons that were supposed to be moved out 20 kilometres away, we moved what could be moved, but what remained was that that was not in working order, because the agreement did not say that units have to be disbanded. That's not what the agreement says. It's only that weaponry has to be handed over to UNPROFOR for safeguarding. So roughly, I did go to these weapon collection points. They had wire around them. Akashi came and Brosse and all these other generals from Zagreb, et cetera. So there was this wire fence around it, and there were weapons that had been decommissioned in the middle, and then, of course, if there was to be an attack of the 1st Corps of the BH Army, they should be combat ready. It's not that they did not hand over their weaponry to UNPROFOR. However, personnel were not. They remained under my command. Let's be clear on that. So we just had these light weapons from 12.7-millimetre calibre downwards. That's it. That's why that kind of order was issued, so that they would be combat ready so -- because I have --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So are you saying that the units with their private weapons were light weapons from 12.7 downwards? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These units that I referred to are these units that handed over these weapons and perhaps part of the unit would have moved 20 kilometres away, however, their area of responsibility remains. They have to defend that area because there's no one else who can come there. It would only be a case of me leaving it altogether and handing it over to the Muslims and saying, "Go ahead, take it." So weapons below 12.7-millimetre calibre and the area should be protected. And nothing new was written here, nothing more than that. Madam Prosecutor, have I provided a sufficient explanation or do you have more questions in this regard?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think I want to show you another document now, General. P01294, and it's dated 12 June 1994. And it's correspondence from General Milovanovic to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we are waiting, if I may be allowed, I think that there is a misunderstanding stemming from the translation "private." I mean a mortar can be private too. However, this is light weaponry, sidearms, infantry weapons. They had not been banned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the paragraph that we just saw, I think it speaks for itself. We can continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this document, General, says -- and it's marked as urgent, says that the Ilijas Brigade had written the Main Staff requesting that they be issued aerial bombs by Pretis, and General Milovanovic cautions you that the Main Staff decides on the use of aerial bombs and possibly a corps if the Main Staff approves. So my question about this document, General, is: Are aerial bombs of a size that were banned according to the total exclusion zone agreement?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a hard question for me because we did not look at that. I'll tell you what, from October 1992, the use of airforce had been banned. This was the so-called no-fly operation. So the use of aerial bombs in a way had been banned there. Whereas this document, I don't know. It never reached me. You see that it went directly to -- well, you asked me, you asked me, so I'm answering.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So if aerial bombs -- if aerial bombs weren't used because there was a no-fly operation, why then is General Milovanovic writing you to say that either he or you, the Main Staff or you, decide on their use in 1994?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is June 1994. At that time we did have these aerial bombs in some of our depots. Now, Josipovic is the commander of the Ilijas Brigade -- no, not the Ilijas Brigade. Yes, it is the Ilijas Brigade. And he's asking for these bombs to be taken out, because we were wondering what to do in a situation when heavy weapons were taken away from us, when in the corps zone we have 10.000 and the 1st Corps has 45.000 rifles, light weapons. If they attack us, what are we going to defend ourselves with. We don't have weapons. Then somebody gave the following proposal: That it would be a good thing to prepare this reserve weaponry. So I did not really take part in these discussions and I cannot tell you about these aerial bombs a lot. I'm really not familiar enough with that problem. So this is a request just to get it out. I mean, I know that there was talk about that, like, "What do we do now? This is the situation we're in." That's why we proposed that this anti-sniper agreement be reached as soon as possible, so that we could stop the 1st Corps of the BH Army if they attack us because we don't have the forces to attack [as interpreted] them because we, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, are left to our own resources and we don't have that. I've already spoken about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You mentioned reserve weaponry. You're talking about reserve weaponry that would use these air-bombs, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. We didn't have anything then, no other weapons. Now, whether there were other weapons or not then, I cannot say whether they constructed something or not. I saw later that something was used but not in my time. As far as I can remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript. Transcript, lines 4, 5. It doesn't record it properly. The General said: If they attack us, we have nothing to defend ourselves with because we no longer have any advantage. Our weapons have been taken away. It's not that we would attack them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I think it will be checked during the review process today. Yes, but before going further, General, how do you know that this document didn't reach you? You stated that it didn't reach you. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't seem to remember it. That's why I say that maybe it hadn't reach know. I cannot remember now. Now that I've read it, I see that Milovanovic wrote it. I cannot remember that it was in my hands. Probably the further processing of that had that taken place. I don't know. Well, I didn't remember. I do not remember that such a document --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not trying to say that it didn't happen. I'm just saying I could not remember. That would be my most sincere answer. I don't know what else to say, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So despite the fact that Milovanovic thought the issue of the use of air-bombs was important enough to write to you urgently, you have no recollection -- your indulgence for a moment. So if nothing was going on with these air-bombs in June of 1994, why did Milovanovic write to you urgently then, General?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can see in the introduction of this document that the brigade commander asked them directly. He didn't ask me. The Main Staff directly. He asked approval from them. That is how I understood this document. If --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Directly. Addressed them directly, the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So then Josipovic must have come to you directly, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The system of any army, I've explained that, is based on singleness of command and subordination. Without that, there can be no army in the world. If it's any different, it's no good. So I'm Josipovic's immediate superior as corps commander, and his second superior is the General Staff or General Mladic, or it's the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So did Josipovic then come to you to ask to use air-bombs?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying I don't remember. I don't remember problems with this regard. Could you please jog my memory if you can.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, that's fine, General. What we'll do is we'll move on to one more and last document for the day. It's 65 ter number 23835. And it's your report on the state of -- dated May 5th, 1994, your report on the state of combat readiness of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps anti-aircraft defence and rocket units.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if you can scroll down to the bottom of this page. I'd then like us all to go to page 5 in English under the heading "Training of Crews," and the same page is page 3 in B/C/S. In the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, under that heading "Training of Crews," second sentence, we see in your report: All compositions fired on targets in combat, whereas only sight-setters and operators fired on air targets in the axes sectors of Ilijas, Breza, and Gorazde, SAM-2 missile operator Koprivica having hit a NATO aircraft. Now, General, at transcript page 37461 you said: "As far as I know and according to information I had, we never opened fire on UN planes." When you said that, I take it you weren't including NATO planes in your answer, then, were you, because you did open fire on NATO planes.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a special situation, Madam Prosecutor. Those forces which were engaged near Gorazde -- could you please remind me of the date? I would like to put things in a context. What date was that? The date. The date of the document. Please remind me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: May 5th, 1994, is the date of the document. My colleague could show you -- take you to the first page of the document again, please, so you can see it.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. No, no. I believe you when you say that that was the case. Let's leave it at that, of course. This is a description of the entire situation and combat readiness. This is also an assessment of the situation in the corps. We had some of the troops that were engaged but they were attached to the forces that were attacking in the direction of Gorazde, and that was as far as I can remember. On the 10th of April, 1994, when NATO staged its first strikes on the positions of Republika Srpska, that was not under my command but under the direct command of the Main Staff, but some of the forces were engaged in Jabucko Sedlo. We had some assault battalions that participated in that part of the operation but not under my command. They were attached to other units. It was said at that time, or at least that's what I was said, that somebody shot an aeroplane down from our contingent. There were other versions. For example, that that was the Russian needle. However, a soldier was named that hit a NATO plane and grounded it. I inquired about that. I wanted to find out whether that was a soldier that needed to be decorated. However, he was not under my command, so it was not up to me to take any measures with this regard. This is my answer to your question whether we shot at NATO, i.e., UNPROFOR airforce, because that part of NATO that patrolled with their aircraft, I consider them to be an integral part of the United Nations because they could not patrol without an approval by the United Nations. They were attacking at the time. That was a situation in which all the agreements had to be called off. This was a battle between the Army of Republika Srpska and NATO in the sector of Gorazde. This was outside of my area of responsibility. I don't know whether I made myself clear, Madam Prosecutor. In other words, that unit was attached to some other contingents, and I believe that they were under the command of a person called Masal [phoen] but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have this document as a Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6304, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I remember that you -- yesterday you stated that you would come back after checking the B/C/S translation of footnote 711.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We have done that Your Honours. The matter has been referred to CLSS and they are dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That was done first thing this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, sir, I'll try to put simpler questions than those during my examination-in-chief. I'm looking for yes and no answers. Let's start with the last things first. Was Gorazde in the total exclusion zone or outside of it?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Outside of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were shown a document, P1294. General Milovanovic warns Colonel Josipovic about his lack of discipline. He is a general now. On from what side was General Josipovic's unit attacked?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I believe that he was a captain. All of my officers were promoted. I was the only one who was demoted. He was a captain. He was not the general. He was the commander of the Ilijas Brigade. His troops were attacked from Visoko, Vares, and Olovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us whether anybody attacked General Josipovic from the total exclusion zone or -- and were those places within the total exclusion zone?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were parts of the Ilijas Brigade that would fall within the 20-kilometre zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The question's been answered. I'll save it for another occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When it comes to the area of Visoko, Breza, Vares, and Olovo, were these places within the total exclusion zone?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And could they attack --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's outside the cross-examination in my submission, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does it not deal with that document, i.e., Exhibit P1294?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In my submission, the document does not refer in any regard to Colonel Josipovic being under attack by anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The subject of the exclusion zone was clearly raised by the Prosecution. They can't limit it that narrowly, so Dr. Karadzic has the right to rebut that by the question that he's asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, the Chamber agrees with Mr. Robinson, so we will allow the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, let's make things simple. Those zones from which Colonel Josipovic was attacked, Visoko, Breza, Vares, and Olovo, were they part of the total exclusion zone?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those zones were excluded. However, one part of the zone of that brigade was within the 20-kilometre zone, looking from the centre of Sarajevo and Marin Dvor, across Vogosca, and further on towards Ilijas. So 20-kilometres would fall within that area in the direction of Visoko. However, Visoko itself was excluded from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that due to the total exclusion zone, it was forbidden to the BiH Army to attack the Ilijas Brigade from Visoko, Breza, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know that much better than I do. You were the one who drafted that agreement. I didn't [as interpreted] attend that, and that did not forbid actions of the BiH Army from those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was Colonel Josipovic prohibited to open fire towards Visoko and the other places which were not within the total exclusion zone?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't, unless there was something -- and I'm talking about a period of time which is very important to emphasise because it is very important whether there was a cease-fire in place, but in general terms, it was not forbidden to open fire in those directions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the two speakers be reminded to slow down and make pauses between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now that both interlocutors are speaking the same time language, please bear in mind that you should put a pause and speak more slowly. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We apologise to the participants and the Trial Chamber as well as the interpreters. I will speak slowly and I will make pauses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On line 2, I would like to correct something in the transcript. You said you did attend the negotiations but that I authored the agreement. Is it true that you attended or not?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the 18th of February. I attended the negotiations, we repeated that several times, but you sign the agreement. You were the Supreme Commander and I wasn't, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When it comes to Mr. Josipovic - and I don't know what his rank was at the time - did he receive what he requested?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he didn't get what he asked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If he had received the assets, would he have been in a position to use them in the direction of the total exclusion zone? Who was his southern neighbour?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Southern or south-eastern, it was the 3rd Sarajevo or the Vogosca Brigade. Even if he had received those assets he did not have the means to use them. How could he have used aerial bombs?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 3rd Sarajevo Brigade, was that a Serbian brigade, this SRK?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 3rd Sarajevo Brigade was set up somewhat later and then merged the Vogosca and Rajlovac and Kosani [phoen] Brigade. And yes, it was the SRK.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 63 of today's transcript you were shown an order and I'm afraid that we are facing a linguistic problem here. Can you tell us is there a difference and what the difference is between a planning order and an executive order? In English it is all translated as "order." However, would you say that there is a difference between various orders? Can you explain that to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a nutshell, when it comes to the execution of combat tasks, the Supreme Command issues directives and lower commands issue combat orders. A combat order or an order for combat activities contains all the elements that concern combat and resistance; whereas orders issued by the other command organs arise from that order and those are professional or expert orders, as it were. They can come from the chief of artillery, the chief of engineers, the assistant for logistics, and so on and so forth. When it comes to planning or plans, plans are the same everywhere and the name is self-explanatory. It has to be either a textual or a graphic. It can be a network planning or -- and I wouldn't go into details because it would take too much time. A plan is a plan. It's not an order. The two things are different. It can be an annex to either an order or a directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do commands and orders have to be executed? And what about plans, do they have to be executed?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already told you, an army, every army, relies on singleness of command and subordination. Singleness of command means that there is one superior officer in command, that there couldn't be two or more commanders. There could be only one and he's responsible. As soon as somebody else interferes, whoever is in charge has to assume responsibility. Subordination, on the other hand, says that a subordinate by rank or by position is duty-bound to carry out orders issued him to by his superior. This is what subordination means. And when it comes to plans and whether they are executed, it depends on the -- on how realistic it is and how viable it is, to use a peacetime term. In wartime, this means that it has to be based on good assessment and the characteristics and the decision of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that His Excellency noticed in P1009 -- and I would like to call up the document. It is P1009, page 3. The title is "Firing Tasks." Page 3, "Firing Tasks," please. This is not the same document. Not the one that we saw under that number previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we see the previous page in B/C/S, while leaving the English as it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here it is. We can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is the document. Now, please, General, tell us what under this first -- prevent the attack of the enemy from Sarajevo aimed at unblocking Sarajevo, opening fire on the sectors of Humsko Brdo, Pofalici, Velesici, and so on. You were asked about this, but please tell us about the fourth paragraph -- the third paragraph, support offensive operations by firing along axis Faletici and so on. Where is that, Faletici, Mrkovici? That's also outside of Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all right. In this order that's not so important because the order emphasises another problem. The axis is specified along which a possible enemy attack is to be expected. Along that axis fire is to be planned. This is why the chief of artillery assesses here that it could be the possible axis of the enemy forces, where they would attack, and the fire is planned. It doesn't have to be carried out. But if the enemy breaks through, then the firing will indeed take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It's not recorded that these localities are outside of Sarajevo. Please look at the fourth one: Neutralise the enemy artillery by opening fire on the follow sectors, Velesici, Pofalici, Bistrik, the tunnel used for transit, Kosevsko Brdo and the Bare cemetery. Was there any Muslim artillery there that needed to be neutralised?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period, the chief of artillery had the information about the exact locations of the enemy artillery and he issued a preparatory order to prepare for fire against those sectors, whether it was automatic fire or concentrated fire, but all circumstances that have to be planned were taken into account. And they had their own artillery reconnaissance which was separate and they would establish the targets. So I need not necessarily know everything as the corps commander. He's the commander or the chief, rather, and he would plan what his duties were.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D3394, can we please see that one briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was suggested to you that Velesici are a civilian settlement. Please look at item number 1 and the second bullet. What was the enemy doing? With combined infantry and artillery fire from the direction of Brek [phoen], Kosevo and Velesici at the Mrkovici village, could the enemy reach Mrkovici by infantry fire from Velesici or was it rather the artillery component?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Velesici, Mr. President, we already discussed Velesici and I expressed my opinion in relation to the earlier report. And this is another confirmation that there were some forces in Velesici. There was a disposition of forces, and it was still expected that there would be fire from that direction, and this confirms that it did come from the area of Velesici. I don't know about the second part of your question. I may have missed it or I didn't answer it. I'm getting tired already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, sir, you have already said that there were civilian settlements in Sarajevo too. Were there civilian settlements which were completely demilitarised from which fire was not opened at you and that you opened fire at such settlements?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, there were civilian areas or zones in which, for example, the forces of the BH Army 1st Corps did not enter, but it was difficult to establish that. We saw from some information that they did not even allow the UNPROFOR to enter and check those areas, let alone that I would go there to see. There were civilian areas where troops were located and they could have become military targets or they did not become military targets. It's hard to give a universal answer, but there were civilian zones, civilian areas, protected zones, safety zones, yes, certainly there were some. We never -- as far as I know, all these protected areas, axes, facilities, we never launched any attacks on them. Yes, we did discuss the Kosevo Hospital quite a lot and the warning, returning fire, when it is a military target, when it's not a military target, which part is a military target. We could expand it if necessary. I can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. It was suggested also to you that Cengic Vila was a civilian settlement. Were there any legitimate military targets in Cengic Vila or any firing positions from which fire was opened at your units?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, was that where the Jajce barracks was located?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Jajce barracks is to the east. That's where the factory Treska was and so on. Do you remember how it looked? We can call up a map.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We don't need to call up anything. I stated here that, in that period, there were some troops moving around Cengic Vila and that some command post was somewhere around there. Now, whether I've been sufficiently clear about that, I'm not sure. I think I have been clear.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
